papers.title: Knowledgeless Language Models: Suppressing Parametric Recall for Evidence-Grounded Language Modeling
papers.abstract: Language models encode substantial factual knowledge in their parameters, which can lead to unreliable behavior when this knowledge is outdated, incomplete, or misaligned with the provided context. In this work, we study whether modifying the pretraining signal can systematically shift models away from parametric recall and toward evidence-grounded reasoning. We introduce Knowledge--''Less'' Language Models (KLLMs), a fundamentally different epistemic training paradigm for LLMs, which are pretrained on corpora in which named entities are anonymized, thereby removing a primary channel for entity-linked factual supervision. This intervention substantially reduces closed-book factual recall, while often improving performance on tasks where relevant information is provided as context. Across multiple model scales, KLLMs consistently outperform matched baselines on contextual question answering, fact verification, and hallucination detection benchmarks. Crucially, in retrieval-grounded settings with imperfect evidence, KLLMs show improved robustness and achieve up to 20--25\% relative gains over standard language models. They further exhibit better calibration, with improved ECE, Brier score, and AUROC, as well as more reliable abstention behavior. Our results demonstrate that suppressing entity-linked supervision during pretraining induces a shift in epistemic behavior: KLLMs rely less on parametric knowledge and more on external evidence, leading to improved reliability under realistic conditions. This suggests that pretraining-time control over knowledge acquisition can complement retrieval-augmented and tool-based systems by providing a more evidence-sensitive base model.

summary.takeaway: Pretraining language models on anonymized corpora reduces parametric factual recall and improves evidence-grounded reasoning, robustness, and calibration.
summary.problem: Language models rely heavily on parametric knowledge, which can be outdated or misaligned, causing unreliable behavior in evidence-grounded tasks.
summary.method: KLLMs are pretrained on corpora with anonymized named entities to suppress entity-linked factual supervision and shift models toward external evidence reliance.
summary.evidence: KLLMs outperform matched baselines by up to 20–25% on retrieval-grounded tasks with imperfect evidence and show improved calibration metrics like ECE, Brier score, and AUROC.
summary.limitations: The paper does not provide detailed quantitative results or ablation studies on the impact of anonymization granularity or downstream task diversity.
summary.why_for_you: This approach offers a novel pretraining paradigm to enhance trustworthy LLM behavior by reducing harmful parametric recall and improving robustness in evidence-grounded applications.

signals.text: KLLMs pretrained on anonymized corpora reduce closed-book factual recall but improve performance on contextual QA, fact verification, and hallucination detection benchmarks.
The anonymization of named entities during pretraining removes a primary channel for entity-linked factual supervision, fundamentally shifting the epistemic behavior of LLMs.
In retrieval-grounded settings with imperfect evidence, KLLMs achieve up to 20–25% relative gains over standard LMs and exhibit better calibration metrics such as ECE, Brier score, and AUROC.

deep_dive.overview: This work addresses the challenge that large language models (LLMs) encode factual knowledge parametrically, which can lead to unreliable outputs when such knowledge is outdated or misaligned with context. The authors propose Knowledge--''Less'' Language Models (KLLMs), which are pretrained on corpora where named entities are anonymized, effectively suppressing entity-linked factual supervision during pretraining. This intervention reduces the model's reliance on parametric recall and encourages evidence-grounded reasoning. Empirical results across multiple model scales demonstrate that KLLMs outperform matched baselines on contextual question answering, fact verification, and hallucination detection tasks. Notably, in retrieval-augmented scenarios with imperfect evidence, KLLMs show substantial robustness improvements, achieving up to 20–25% relative gains. Additionally, KLLMs exhibit better calibration and more reliable abstention behavior, indicating improved trustworthiness. These findings suggest that controlling knowledge acquisition during pretraining can complement retrieval and tool-based methods by producing base models that are more sensitive to external evidence, thereby enhancing reliability in realistic settings.

mechanism.detail: By anonymizing named entities during pretraining, the model's primary channel for learning entity-linked factual knowledge is removed. This shifts the model's epistemic behavior from relying on memorized facts to depending more on external evidence provided at inference time. No explicit equations or causal models are provided.

papers.title: Verifier-Based Reinforcement Fine-Tuning of Reasoning Models for Thermal Energy Storage Control
papers.abstract: Buildings are expected to shift cooling loads in response to grid conditions. Thermal energy storage (TES) enables this shift, but scheduling it well requires planning hours ahead under storage constraints. Model predictive control (MPC) and reinforcement learning are difficult to scale across buildings. This study instead adapts an open-weight reasoning model through reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). We convert exact offline dynamic-programming (DP) action values into dense rewards for every candidate action. Using only 30 training prompts, reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) trains the model as an upper-level scheduler that outputs hourly heat-pump setpoints from text-based states and forecasts. Evaluation uses a deliberately simple office-building TES benchmark where exact DP is tractable and the optimum is known. RFT reduces the open-weight model's emissions from 70.5 to 61.2 kg-CO2, close to the DP optimum of 60.8 kg-CO2. GPT-5 nearly matches DP and MPC without task-specific training, while GPT-4o, a non-reasoning LLM, produces higher emissions than the no-storage baseline, so inference-time reasoning appears important. Trace analysis shows that RFT mainly stabilizes observable planning patterns (candidate comparison, look-ahead, and feasibility checking) rather than creating a new strategy. Robustness and generalization tests clarify what transfers: the reinforced planning patterns persist under forecast errors and an unseen TES condition and carry over to a battery task, but its different structure limits the gains. DP-based verifiable rewards offer a practical way to adapt open-weight reasoning models to building storage scheduling. These results motivate higher-fidelity tests of whole-building control and scalable verifiers for city-scale energy management.

summary.takeaway: Reinforcement fine-tuning with dynamic programming-based verifiable rewards effectively adapts open-weight reasoning models for thermal energy storage scheduling, achieving near-optimal emissions reduction.
summary.problem: Efficiently scheduling thermal energy storage in buildings requires scalable planning under storage constraints, which is challenging for model predictive control and reinforcement learning methods.
summary.method: The study uses reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards derived from exact offline dynamic programming action values to fine-tune an open-weight reasoning model as an upper-level scheduler.
summary.evidence: Reinforcement fine-tuning reduces emissions from 70.5 to 61.2 kg-CO2, closely approaching the dynamic programming optimum of 60.8 kg-CO2 on a simple TES benchmark.
summary.limitations: The approach’s gains are limited when transferring to structurally different tasks like battery control, and higher-fidelity tests on whole-building control remain to be conducted.
summary.why_for_you: This work demonstrates a practical method to leverage verifiable rewards for efficient adversarial training of reasoning LLMs in energy management, relevant for trustworthy and scalable LLM control applications.

signals.text: Reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) stabilizes planning patterns such as candidate comparison, look-ahead, and feasibility checking rather than inventing new strategies, indicating the model learns to reliably execute known reasoning steps.

The method converts exact offline dynamic programming (DP) action values into dense, verifiable rewards for every candidate action, enabling precise reinforcement learning signal without requiring extensive training data.

Evaluation on a simple office-building TES benchmark shows RFT reduces emissions from 70.5 to 61.2 kg-CO2, nearly matching the DP optimum of 60.8 kg-CO2, while GPT-4o without reasoning produces worse emissions than no storage.

deep_dive.overview: This paper addresses the challenge of scheduling thermal energy storage (TES) in buildings to shift cooling loads efficiently under storage constraints, a task difficult for traditional model predictive control (MPC) and reinforcement learning due to scalability issues. The authors propose reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), leveraging exact offline dynamic programming (DP) action values as dense rewards to fine-tune an open-weight reasoning model. Using only 30 training prompts, reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) trains the model to output hourly heat-pump setpoints from text-based states and forecasts. The approach is evaluated on a simple TES benchmark where the DP optimum is known, demonstrating that RFT achieves emissions close to the optimum and outperforms non-reasoning LLMs. Trace analysis reveals that RFT stabilizes existing planning patterns rather than creating new strategies. Robustness tests show these reinforced patterns generalize under forecast errors and to an unseen TES condition, with partial transfer to a battery control task. The study highlights DP-based verifiable rewards as a practical adaptation mechanism for reasoning models in building storage scheduling, motivating future work on higher-fidelity and scalable energy management applications.

papers.title: Can LLMs Write Reliable Rubrics? A Meta-Evaluation for Experiment Reproduction
papers.abstract: Rubric-based evaluation is a promising approach for assessing open-ended outputs from LLM-based research agents, particularly in paper reproduction, where direct paper-to-repository comparison is prone to hallucination. However, constructing paper-specific rubrics requires substantial expert effort, limiting the scalability of benchmarks such as PaperBench. In this work, we present, to our knowledge, the first systematic meta-evaluation of LLM-generated rubrics for paper reproduction. We reformulate rubrics into a checklist-style format and evaluate four generation settings across two backbone models. We meta-evaluate generated rubrics intrinsically by semantic similarity and extrinsically by score alignment with ground-truth rubrics. Our results show that the augmented settings substantially improves downstream evaluation alignment, with the strongest setting approaching the human baseline, while intrinsic gains are more modest. Further analyses reveal that LLM-generated rubrics are often overly fine-grained, biased toward high scores, and less adaptive to paper domains, highlighting both the affordances and limitations.

summary.takeaway: Augmented LLM-generated rubrics substantially improve alignment with human evaluation in paper reproduction tasks, nearing human baseline performance.
summary.problem: Constructing paper-specific rubrics for evaluating LLM-based paper reproduction is expert-intensive and limits benchmark scalability.
summary.method: The study meta-evaluates LLM-generated rubrics reformulated into checklist format across four generation settings and two backbone models using intrinsic semantic similarity and extrinsic score alignment.
summary.evidence: Augmented rubric generation settings show substantial improvement in downstream evaluation alignment, with the best setting approaching human baseline, despite modest intrinsic semantic gains.
summary.limitations: LLM-generated rubrics tend to be overly fine-grained, biased toward high scores, and less adaptive to diverse paper domains.
summary.why_for_you: This work provides critical insights into automating rubric generation for trustworthy evaluation of LLM research agents, addressing hallucination-prone direct comparisons.

signals.text: The strongest augmented rubric generation setting achieves downstream evaluation alignment close to human baseline, demonstrating effective rubric automation for paper reproduction.
Rubrics are reformulated into a checklist-style format and evaluated across four generation settings and two backbone LLMs, enabling systematic meta-evaluation of rubric quality.
Intrinsic evaluation via semantic similarity shows only modest gains, indicating that semantic closeness alone is insufficient to guarantee evaluation alignment.

deep_dive.overview: This paper addresses the challenge of scalable, reliable evaluation of LLM-generated research outputs in paper reproduction tasks, where direct comparison to repositories is prone to hallucination. The authors propose automating rubric generation using LLMs and conduct the first systematic meta-evaluation of these rubrics. They convert rubrics into checklist-style formats and test four generation settings across two backbone models. Evaluation is twofold: intrinsic semantic similarity and extrinsic score alignment with ground-truth rubrics. Results reveal that augmented rubric generation settings significantly improve downstream evaluation alignment, nearly matching human baselines, while intrinsic semantic similarity gains remain modest. Further analysis uncovers that LLM-generated rubrics are often overly detailed, biased toward higher scores, and less adaptable across paper domains. These findings highlight both the potential and current limitations of LLM-generated rubrics for trustworthy, scalable evaluation in LLM-based research agent benchmarks.

papers.title: The Illusion of Robustness: Aggregate Accuracy Hides Prediction Flips under Task-Irrelevant Context
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) grow more capable, they are increasingly deployed in context-rich settings where task inputs are often accompanied by long, partially irrelevant context. In a controlled setting, we find that state-of-the-art models often appear robust to task-irrelevant context at the aggregate level: prepending it to benchmark questions causes little change in overall accuracy. This aggregate stability, however, masks significant per-example instability. Even semantically meaningless pseudo-words, formed by randomly combining characters, can markedly shift model predictions on a small fraction of examples, degrading performance on some while improving it on others. This two-sided effect holds consistently across a wide range of models and datasets, yet the affected examples are largely model-specific. We further show that this instability is modulated by context type, context length, test-time compute, and model development stage. Together, our findings reveal context-induced tail risks concealed by aggregate accuracy, motivating per-example reliability evaluation of language models.

summary.takeaway: Aggregate accuracy metrics obscure significant per-example prediction instability caused by task-irrelevant context in state-of-the-art LLMs.
summary.problem: LLMs deployed with long, partially irrelevant context appear robust at the aggregate level but exhibit unstable predictions on individual examples.
summary.method: The study prepends task-irrelevant context, including semantically meaningless pseudo-words, to benchmark questions and analyzes prediction changes across multiple models and datasets.
summary.evidence: Prepending pseudo-words shifts model predictions on a small fraction of examples, with effects varying by context type, length, compute, and model development stage.
summary.limitations: The analysis is limited to controlled settings and does not provide mechanistic explanations for the observed instability.
summary.why_for_you: Understanding per-example prediction flips under irrelevant context is critical for trustworthy LLM deployment in real-world, context-rich environments.

signals.text: State-of-the-art LLMs show stable aggregate accuracy when irrelevant context is prepended, yet individual examples experience significant prediction flips.
The method uses semantically meaningless pseudo-words formed by random character combinations to isolate the effect of irrelevant context on model predictions.
Prediction instability is modulated by factors including context type, context length, test-time compute, and model development stage, indicating nuanced sensitivity.

deep_dive.overview: This research investigates the robustness of large language models to task-irrelevant context by prepending such context to benchmark questions and measuring prediction stability. While aggregate accuracy remains largely unchanged, the study reveals significant per-example prediction flips, including both degradations and improvements, when irrelevant context is introduced. The use of pseudo-words as irrelevant context isolates semantic effects, demonstrating that even meaningless input can alter model behavior. This instability is consistent across diverse models and datasets but affects examples in a model-specific manner. Furthermore, the degree of instability depends on context characteristics and model factors such as development stage and computational budget at test time. These findings expose hidden tail risks in LLM reliability that aggregate metrics fail to capture, underscoring the need for per-example evaluation to ensure trustworthy deployment in context-rich scenarios.

Can model design or training be adapted to reduce context-induced tail risks without sacrificing aggregate accuracy?

papers.title: LLM Judges Can Be Too Generous When There Is No Reference Answer
papers.abstract: LLM judges are increasingly being used to evaluate open-ended model responses, often in no-reference settings where a ground-truth answer is unavailable. However, can they reliably assess in such evaluation setups? We explore this question in this paper through a two stage pipeline with a) calibration experiments that assess the judge model's knowledge of the task it is evaluating, and b) sensitivity experiments that assess how the judge model's performance is impacted by the presence and positioning of the reference answer in the prompt. Across experiments covering three languages, we show that the judge models we evaluated tend to over-credit incorrect answers in the absence of a reference answer, and adding reference answer information to the prompt flips the judge model's correct/incorrect decisions by as much as 85% in some experimental settings. Comparison with a subset of human annotations shows that these reference-driven changes generally align with human judgments. Our results emphasize the need for calibrating the LLM judges with a sample with reference-aware evaluation before using them in reference-free setups reliably, and our methodology provides a blueprint for researchers and practitioners in doing such calibration of LLM judges for other tasks.

summary.takeaway: LLM judges tend to over-credit incorrect answers without reference answers, and their decisions shift drastically when reference answers are included.
summary.problem: Can LLM judges reliably evaluate open-ended model responses in no-reference settings where ground-truth answers are unavailable?
summary.method: A two-stage pipeline involving calibration experiments to assess judge model task knowledge and sensitivity experiments to measure impact of reference answer presence and positioning.
summary.evidence: Experiments across three languages show up to 85% flips in judge decisions when reference answers are added, aligning with human annotations.
summary.limitations: The study does not provide quantitative metrics beyond decision flip rates or detailed analysis of judge model architectures.
summary.why_for_you: Understanding and calibrating LLM judges is critical for trustworthy evaluation of open-ended LLM outputs in reference-free scenarios.

signals.text: LLM judges over-credit incorrect answers in no-reference settings, indicating a systematic bias in their evaluation without ground-truth context.
The two-stage pipeline includes calibration experiments to verify judge model task knowledge and sensitivity experiments to test how reference answer presence affects judgments.
Adding reference answers to prompts causes up to 85% of judge model decisions to flip between correct and incorrect, demonstrating high sensitivity to reference information.

deep_dive.overview: This paper investigates the reliability of large language model (LLM) judges when evaluating open-ended responses without access to ground-truth reference answers. The authors propose a two-stage evaluation pipeline: first, calibration experiments assess whether the judge model understands the task it is evaluating; second, sensitivity experiments measure how the presence and positioning of reference answers in the prompt influence the judge's decisions. Conducted across three languages, the experiments reveal that LLM judges systematically over-credit incorrect answers when no reference is provided. Introducing reference answers into the prompt causes dramatic shifts in evaluation outcomes, with up to 85% of decisions flipping from correct to incorrect or vice versa. These shifts align well with human annotations, suggesting that reference-aware calibration is essential for trustworthy LLM judging. The methodology offers a practical blueprint for calibrating LLM judges before deploying them in no-reference evaluation settings, addressing a critical gap in reliable automated evaluation of open-ended LLM outputs.

methodology.detail: These experiments assess the judge model's understanding of the evaluation task by testing its ability to correctly judge responses when reference answers are present, ensuring the model has task-relevant knowledge before no-reference evaluation.

methodology.title: Sensitivity Experiments
methodology.detail: These experiments evaluate how the judge model's decisions change when reference answers are added or repositioned in the prompt, quantifying the impact of reference information on judgment reliability.

mechanism.title: No explicit mechanism provided
mechanism.detail: The paper does not present a formal mechanism or theoretical model explaining why LLM judges over-credit incorrect answers without references or why reference presence causes decision flips.

experiments.title: Multilingual Evaluation

findings.title: Over-crediting Incorrect Answers
findings.detail: LLM judges tend to assign credit to incorrect model responses when no reference answer is provided, indicating unreliable evaluation in no-reference settings.

findings.title: High Sensitivity to Reference Answers
findings.detail: Inclusion of reference answers in prompts causes up to 85% of judge decisions to flip, demonstrating that reference information strongly influences evaluation outcomes.

findings.title: Alignment with Human Judgments
findings.detail: Changes in judge decisions driven by reference answer presence generally align with human annotations, validating the importance of reference-aware calibration.

contributions: Identification of systematic over-crediting by LLM judges in no-reference evaluation settings.
Development of a two-stage pipeline combining calibration and sensitivity experiments to assess judge reliability.
Empirical demonstration of up to 85% decision flips caused by reference answer inclusion across three languages.
Provision of a practical methodology blueprint for calibrating LLM judges before no-reference deployment.
limitations: Lack of detailed quantitative metrics beyond decision flip percentages limits understanding of judge accuracy.
No analysis of the impact of different judge model architectures or sizes on evaluation reliability.
Absence of a formal theoretical mechanism explaining observed judge behavior.
Limited information on dataset specifics or task domains used in experiments.
open_questions: How do different LLM judge architectures or training regimes affect over-crediting behavior in no-reference settings?
Can formal theoretical models explain why reference answers cause large decision flips in LLM judges?
What are effective calibration strategies to improve judge reliability across diverse tasks and languages?
How does judge performance vary with different types of open-ended tasks beyond those tested?
